coherence.reasons: Both run a clean hierarchy from governing thought to recommendation. Y's governing thought splits into three pillars (enter rather than Japan; Amazon rather than retail; launch with conditions), and every slide title maps to one of them, with a 'so what' tying each page back. Its seven-condition test of the CEO's hypothesis sets up the later sections directly. X's storyline is also logical (prize, retail fails, Amazon passes, risks, how to launch) and its executive summary mirrors the slides. But X has a small internal tension: its backup says to 'use 32%' as ACoS at scale, while the headline case is 'passes on plan' with a ceiling set exactly at the 28.6% break-even. Y states the same tension more directly ('passes, but with little room on payback') and carries it through to the gate design.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation: Amazon-led with gates, retail only above 20% awareness, and the $40M ambition reset. Both reject Option B on the board's own constraints. Y weighs the trade-offs more fully. It states the Japan trade-off outright (Japan is safer for 2030 cash, +$1.8M against −$2.3M at benchmark ACoS) and proposes revisiting Japan for 2028. It frames ambition versus constraints as a formal board choice and recommends which gives way. It sets the ACoS ceiling at 28%, below the 28.6% break-even, and says to give up growth rather than buy volume above the ceiling. Its March 2028 gate has green/amber/red rules with derived thresholds (at least 96% of plan volume at 28% ACoS; stop above 32% ACoS or below 70% of volume) and a quantified loss if stopped (about $3M). X's gates are sound but softer. Its ceiling sits exactly at break-even with no margin, the response to a miss is 'cut spend on weakest keywords', and there is no explicit stop rule beyond an end-2027 review. X treats Japan more briefly ('safe, but builds no US business') and leaves the path to $40M as 'after retail' without the board-choice framing.

evidence.reasons: Both get the required calculations right: $10.72 and $4.73 Amazon contribution, $7.54–7.55 retail contribution, Option B peak of $20.8M, 4.5% group margin, payback at 25/28/32% ACoS of +$2.4M/+$0.4M/−$2.3M, the 28.6% break-even, and 26.9% under the higher tariff. Both avoid the traps: the $5.2B figure, the 4.5 units per door, the halo correlation, and Saebom survivorship. X adds the 28% ACoS plus tariff case (−$0.7M), which matches the key. Y goes further on the critical evidence. It runs an ACoS × volume grid, shows the halo would need to be 2.1–3.4× to pay for retail, models evidence-adjusted Option B (−$26.4M), models the CEO's 2029 retail phase (−$11.8M, 6.3% margin), and quantifies FX. It also notes that pilot growth decelerated from 16–17% to 8–9% a month, which bears on the trap of treating pilot growth as permanent, and it uses the 52% price-sensitivity finding. Y's weak spots are an illustrative 25% a year path to $40M by 2032 (flagged as not in the data) and a mild 'waiting cedes the market' argument. X's weak spot is the claim that demand grew 'without Onsoo pushing it' with 'little paid push', which is thin given the 28% ACoS. Neither has a material numerical error.

revision.reasons: Both keep the CEO's Amazon-first hypothesis with conditions, which is the expected handling. Both raise the retail trigger from 15% to 20% using the 3.5 median against the 4.0 cut-off, replace the 25% ACoS assumption with a ceiling, and reset the $40M date. X does this in a clear from-to slide covering six changes. Y is more rigorous. It breaks the hypothesis into seven 'what would have to be true' conditions with explicit verdicts. It also quantifies the CEO's second phase: 600 doors from 2029 at the national cost base would take cumulative cash to −$11.8M and group margin to 6.3%, breaking payback and the floor even at above-20% sell-through. From that it adds two conditions X lacks: retail only after payback, and on a door-scaled cost base. X keeps 'retest retail from 2029' without testing whether that timing is compatible with the payback rule.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, numerically accurate documents that reach the defensible recommendation and meet all four defensibility criteria. Y would serve the board better. It tests the CEO's hypothesis condition by condition, including the 2029 retail phase that X leaves unquantified. It makes the Japan and ambition-versus-constraints trade-offs explicit as board choices. It adds volume sensitivity to the ACoS analysis. And its gates are operational: a ceiling below break-even, a dated gate with stop, hold and scale rules, and a sized cash envelope. X is solid and somewhat more cautious about the post-2030 path, but its gates are looser and its treatment of alternatives thinner.
